Computer vision · Technical article

Classical Computer Vision

Edges, corners, descriptors, matching, registration, optical flow, segmentation, shape, texture and the Hough transform: the hand-designed algorithms that do much of the work in vision systems, built from image geometry and signal processing. Each one is written from scratch, checked against OpenCV or scikit-image, and measured on images where the right answer is known.

12 sections47 exercisesPython · NumPy · OpenCV · scikit-imageCode run, outputs shownExercises with solutionsVancouver references

Before networks learned their own features, every part of a vision system was designed by hand. Someone decided that an edge is where the intensity gradient peaks, that a corner is where the gradient points in two directions, that two views of the same point can be recognised by a histogram of nearby gradient orientations, and that a straight line can be found by letting every edge pixel vote for the lines that pass through it. These decisions came from geometry, signal processing and statistics, and the algorithms that follow from them are still everywhere: in camera calibration, panorama stitching, visual odometry, document scanners, industrial inspection, medical image registration, and the preprocessing and post-processing around almost every learned model [1,2].

This article covers the ten families of methods that make up the classical toolkit. They are not ten independent topics. Most share one pipeline (Figure 1): smooth the image and take derivatives (§1), find edges (§2) or distinctive points (§3), describe the neighbourhood of each point (§4), match descriptors between images (§5), and fit a geometric transformation to the matches while rejecting outliers (§6). Optical flow (§7) is the dense, small-motion version of the same correspondence problem. A second branch groups pixels rather than matching them: thresholding, region growing and watershed (§8), measurement of the resulting regions (§9), description of their texture (§10), and voting for parametric shapes (§11). Section 12 assembles the pieces into a working document scanner and discusses where classical methods still win against learned ones.

How this article relates to the rest of the series

Some of this ground is covered elsewhere in the series, and this article cross-references it rather than repeating it. The derivation of the optical flow constraint and a dense one-scale Lucas–Kanade implementation are in Core Computer Vision Tasks §6.1; here §7 adds Horn–Schunck, image pyramids, KLT tracking and a scored comparison. Homographies, the direct linear transform (DLT) and the epipolar geometry that registration relies on are derived in Through the Pinhole (camera models and 3-D geometry); §6 uses them and adds robust estimation. How tracked points feed multi-object trackers and Kalman filters is in Video Understanding and Tracking. Learned replacements for each classical component are the subject of Deep Learning for Vision.

Setup

Every code block marked ran was executed for this article with Python 3.13.17, NumPy 2.5.3 [3], OpenCV 5.0.0 (the opencv-contrib-python-headless wheel) [4], scikit-image 0.26.0 [5], SciPy 1.18.1 and Matplotlib 3.11.2, and its output is pasted verbatim below it. The test images are the public sample images that ship with scikit-image (the cameraman, astronaut, coins, brick, grass, gravel, horse and Hubble deep field images), plus synthetic images generated by the code, which is how most experiments obtain exact ground truth. The code favours clarity over speed: each algorithm is written out in NumPy, then compared with the library implementation you would use in production.

pip install numpy scipy opencv-contrib-python-headless scikit-image matplotlib

§1Images as signals: filtering and scale

A greyscale image is a function I(x, y) sampled on a grid. Almost every classical method begins by applying a linear shift-invariant filter to it: each output pixel is a weighted sum of the input pixels around it, with the same weights everywhere. Written as a correlation with a kernel k,

(I ⊗ k)(x, y) = Σ_u Σ_v k(u, v) · I(x + u, y + v)

Convolution is the same operation with the kernel flipped; for the symmetric kernels used for smoothing the two coincide, and libraries such as OpenCV's filter2D in fact compute correlation [2]. Three filters matter more than all others.

  • The Gaussian Gσ(x, y) = exp(−(x² + y²)/2σ²)/(2πσ²) smooths noise. It is the only kernel that does not create new extrema as σ grows, which is why it defines the scale space L(x, y; σ) = Gσ ⊗ I: a family of ever-blurrier copies in which structures of size about σ are visible [6,7]. It is also separable, the outer product of two 1-D Gaussians, so a k × k kernel costs 2k rather than k² operations per pixel.
  • Derivative filters estimate ∂I/∂x and ∂I/∂y. Because differentiation amplifies noise, they are always combined with smoothing: the derivative of a Gaussian, or its 3 × 3 approximation, the Sobel operator (§2).
  • The Laplacian of Gaussian ∇²Gσ responds to blobs of radius about √2 σ and has zero crossings at edges. The difference of two Gaussians at nearby scales approximates it cheaply.

Two further tools recur. An image pyramid stores the image at successively halved resolutions, each smoothed before subsampling; the Laplacian pyramid stores the band-pass differences between levels [8]. Coarse-to-fine search on a pyramid is how optical flow (§7) and registration (§6) handle large motion. An integral image stores at each pixel the sum of all pixels above and to the left, so the sum over any axis-aligned box costs four lookups regardless of its size. Viola and Jones used it for real-time face detection with Haar-like box features [9], and SURF uses it to approximate Gaussian derivatives with box filters (§4).

filters.pycorrelation, separable Gaussians, denoising, integral images ran

"""Linear filtering from scratch: convolution, separable Gaussians, integral images."""
import time
import numpy as np
import cv2
from skimage import data


def conv2d(img, k):
    """Direct 2-D correlation with reflected borders (what cv2.filter2D computes)."""
    kh, kw = k.shape
    ph, pw = kh // 2, kw // 2
    p = np.pad(img, ((ph, ph), (pw, pw)), mode="reflect")   # reflect = OpenCV's BORDER_REFLECT_101
    out = np.zeros_like(img, dtype=np.float64)
    for dy in range(kh):                                      # loop over the kernel, not the image
        for dx in range(kw):
            out += k[dy, dx] * p[dy:dy + img.shape[0], dx:dx + img.shape[1]]
    return out


def gaussian_kernel1d(sigma):
    r = int(np.ceil(3 * sigma))                               # +-3 sigma holds 99.7% of the mass
    x = np.arange(-r, r + 1)
    g = np.exp(-x ** 2 / (2 * sigma ** 2))
    return g / g.sum()


def integral_image(img):
    """ii[y, x] = sum of img[:y, :x]; one extra zero row and column."""
    return np.pad(img.astype(np.float64).cumsum(0).cumsum(1), ((1, 0), (1, 0)))


def box_sum(ii, y0, x0, y1, x1):
    """Sum over img[y0:y1, x0:x1] with four lookups, whatever the box size."""
    return ii[y1, x1] - ii[y0, x1] - ii[y1, x0] + ii[y0, x0]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    img = data.camera().astype(np.float64) / 255.0

    # 1. direct correlation agrees with OpenCV
    k = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=(5, 5))
    mine = conv2d(img, k)
    ref = cv2.filter2D(img, cv2.CV_64F, k, borderType=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)
    print(f"conv2d vs cv2.filter2D   max |diff| = {np.abs(mine - ref).max():.2e}")

    # 2. a 2-D Gaussian is the outer product of two 1-D Gaussians
    s = 3.0
    g = gaussian_kernel1d(s)
    conv2d(img, g[None, :])                                   # warm-up before timing
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); full = conv2d(img, np.outer(g, g)); t_full = time.perf_counter() - t0
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); sep = conv2d(conv2d(img, g[None, :]), g[:, None]); t_sep = time.perf_counter() - t0
    print(f"Gaussian sigma={s}: kernel {g.size}x{g.size}, {g.size**2} taps vs 2x{g.size} separable")
    print(f"separable vs full        max |diff| = {np.abs(full - sep).max():.2e}"
          f"   time {t_full*1e3:.0f} ms vs {t_sep*1e3:.0f} ms")

    # 3. smoothing removes noise: PSNR before/after
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
    noisy = np.clip(img + rng.normal(0, 0.1, img.shape), 0, 1)
    def psnr(a, b): return 10 * np.log10(1.0 / np.mean((a - b) ** 2))
    print(f"PSNR noisy {psnr(noisy, img):.2f} dB", end="")
    for s in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0):
        sm = cv2.GaussianBlur(noisy, (0, 0), s)
        print(f" | sigma {s}: {psnr(sm, img):.2f} dB", end="")
    print()

    # 4. integral image: any box sum in O(1)
    ii = integral_image(img)
    print(f"box sum via 4 lookups = {box_sum(ii, 100, 50, 300, 450):.4f}"
          f"   direct = {img[100:300, 50:450].sum():.4f}")
conv2d vs cv2.filter2D max |diff| = 0.00e+00 Gaussian sigma=3.0: kernel 19x19, 361 taps vs 2x19 separable separable vs full max |diff| = 2.66e-15 time 232 ms vs 18 ms PSNR noisy 20.45 dB | sigma 0.5: 24.05 dB | sigma 1.0: 27.17 dB | sigma 2.0: 25.41 dB | sigma 4.0: 22.98 dB box sum via 4 lookups = 32879.7922 direct = 32879.7922

The output makes three points. The direct implementation reproduces OpenCV exactly, including the border rule (reflect without repeating the edge pixel, OpenCV's default). Separating the 19 × 19 Gaussian gives the same result to rounding error, eight times faster even in this unoptimised loop. And smoothing is a trade-off: a little blur removes noise faster than it removes detail, so the PSNR rises from 20.5 dB to 27.2 dB at σ = 1, but beyond that blur destroys more image than noise. Figure 2 shows the filters on the test image.

Exercises · §1
  1. A 1920 × 1080 frame is smoothed with a 25 × 25 Gaussian. How many multiply-adds does the direct 2-D filter need, and how many does the separable version need?
    Show solution

    The frame has 2,073,600 pixels. Direct filtering needs 625 multiply-adds per pixel, about 1.30 × 10⁹ in total. Separable filtering needs 25 for the horizontal pass and 25 for the vertical, 50 per pixel, about 1.04 × 10⁸: a 12.5-fold saving that grows linearly with the kernel width.

  2. Smoothing with σ₁ = 3 and then with σ₂ = 4 is equivalent to smoothing once with which σ? Why does this property matter for building a scale space?
    Show solution

    Gaussians compose by adding variances: σ = √(9 + 16) = 5. This semigroup property means each level of a scale space can be computed from the previous level with a small incremental blur, rather than from the original image with an ever larger kernel, and it guarantees that the coarse levels are a pure function of the fine ones [7]. SIFT's pyramid is built this way (§3).

  3. For the 2 × 2 image [[1, 2], [3, 4]], write out the integral image with its zero row and column and use the four-lookup formula to get the sum of the bottom row.
    Show solution

    The padded integral image is [[0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 3], [0, 4, 10]]. The bottom row is the box rows [1, 2) by columns [0, 2), so its sum is ii[2, 2] − ii[1, 2] − ii[2, 0] + ii[1, 0] = 10 − 3 − 0 + 0 = 7 = 3 + 4.

  4. In the output, PSNR peaks at σ = 1 and falls at σ = 4. Explain this in terms of bias and variance, and say how the best σ should change if the noise standard deviation doubles.
    Show solution

    Averaging over a region of about σ² pixels reduces the noise variance roughly in proportion to 1/σ² (less variance), but it also replaces each pixel by a weighted mean of its neighbours, which differ from it near edges and texture (more bias). The error is minimised where the two balance. With stronger noise the variance term matters more, so the optimum moves to a larger σ. Edge-preserving filters such as the bilateral filter or non-local means avoid much of the bias by averaging only over similar pixels, at extra cost [1].

§2Edge detection: Sobel, Canny, Laplacian of Gaussian

An edge is a place where image intensity changes sharply, usually because of a depth discontinuity, a change of surface orientation or material, or a shadow boundary. In one dimension a step edge is a peak of the first derivative and a zero crossing of the second, and the two classical families of detectors follow those two definitions.

2.1 Gradient operators

The gradient ∇I = (Ix, Iy) points across the edge, and its magnitude |∇I| measures the contrast. The Sobel operator estimates Ix with the kernel

⎡ −1 0 +1 ⎤ ⎡ 1 ⎤ S_x = ⎢ −2 0 +2 ⎥ = smoothing ⊗ diff = ⎢ 2 ⎥ · [ −1 0 +1 ] ⎣ −1 0 +1 ⎦ ⎣ 1 ⎦

a central difference in x combined with a small triangular smoothing in y, with Sy = SxT [10]. Thresholding |∇I| gives thick, broken edges and is very sensitive to noise. Canny turned edge detection into an optimisation problem with three criteria: detect real edges and few false ones, locate them accurately, and respond only once to each edge. For a step edge in white noise the optimal filter is closely approximated by the derivative of a Gaussian, and the single response is obtained by keeping only local maxima of the gradient magnitude along the gradient direction [11].

2.2 The Laplacian of Gaussian

Marr and Hildreth proposed the second-derivative route: smooth with a Gaussian, apply the Laplacian ∇² = ∂²/∂x² + ∂²/∂y², and mark the zero crossings [12]. The two steps combine into one isotropic kernel, the Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG), nicknamed the Mexican hat. Zero crossings always form closed contours, which is elegant but also means they include spurious contours in smoothly shaded regions unless they are filtered by the local slope. Marr and Hildreth also noted that a difference of two Gaussians with σ ratio about 1.6 is a close approximation of the LoG; the same approximation reappears in SIFT (§3).

edges.pySobel, Canny and LoG from scratch, scored against exact edges ran

"""Edge detectors from scratch (Sobel, Canny, LoG) and a scored comparison on a synthetic scene."""
import numpy as np
import cv2
from scipy import ndimage as ndi
from skimage import data

SOBEL_X = np.array([[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]], float)


def sobel(img):
    gx = cv2.filter2D(img, cv2.CV_64F, SOBEL_X)
    gy = cv2.filter2D(img, cv2.CV_64F, SOBEL_X.T)
    return gx, gy


def nonmax_suppress(mag, gx, gy):
    """Keep a pixel only if it is a local maximum along the gradient direction (4 bins)."""
    ang = (np.rad2deg(np.arctan2(gy, gx)) + 180) % 180
    H, W = mag.shape
    out = np.zeros_like(mag)
    m = np.pad(mag, 1)
    # neighbour offsets for 0, 45, 90, 135 degrees (rows grow downwards)
    offs = {0: (0, 1), 45: (1, 1), 90: (1, 0), 135: (1, -1)}
    b = (np.round(ang / 45).astype(int) % 4) * 45
    for d, (dy, dx) in offs.items():
        sel = b == d
        n1 = m[1 + dy:1 + dy + H, 1 + dx:1 + dx + W]
        n2 = m[1 - dy:1 - dy + H, 1 - dx:1 - dx + W]
        keep = sel & (mag >= n1) & (mag >= n2)
        out[keep] = mag[keep]
    return out


def hysteresis(nms, lo, hi):
    """Keep weak edges (> lo) only if they are 8-connected to a strong edge (> hi)."""
    weak = nms > lo
    lab, n = ndi.label(weak, structure=np.ones((3, 3)))
    strong_labels = np.unique(lab[nms > hi])
    return np.isin(lab, strong_labels[strong_labels > 0])


def canny(img, sigma, lo, hi):
    sm = cv2.GaussianBlur(img, (0, 0), sigma)
    gx, gy = sobel(sm)
    mag = np.hypot(gx, gy)
    return hysteresis(nonmax_suppress(mag, gx, gy), lo, hi)


def log_edges(img, sigma, thresh):
    """Marr-Hildreth: zero crossings of the Laplacian of Gaussian with enough contrast."""
    L = ndi.gaussian_laplace(img, sigma)
    zc = np.zeros(img.shape, bool)
    for dy, dx in ((0, 1), (1, 0)):
        a, b = L[:L.shape[0] - dy, :L.shape[1] - dx], L[dy:, dx:]
        z = (np.sign(a) != np.sign(b)) & (np.abs(a - b) > thresh)
        zc[:L.shape[0] - dy, :L.shape[1] - dx] |= z
    return zc


def score(pred, gt, tol=1):
    """Precision/recall with a tolerance of `tol` pixels (distance transform matching)."""
    d_gt = ndi.distance_transform_edt(~gt)
    d_pr = ndi.distance_transform_edt(~pred)
    p = (d_gt[pred] <= tol).mean() if pred.any() else 0.0
    r = (d_pr[gt] <= tol).mean()
    return p, r, 2 * p * r / (p + r + 1e-12)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # --- 1. our Canny against OpenCV's on a real photo
    cam = data.camera()
    sm = cv2.GaussianBlur(cam, (0, 0), 1.4)
    ours = canny(cam.astype(float), 1.4, 40, 100)
    ref = cv2.Canny(sm, 40, 100, L2gradient=True) > 0
    p, r, f = score(ours, ref, tol=1)
    print(f"camera: ours {ours.sum()} edge px, cv2.Canny {ref.sum()} px;"
          f" agreement within 1 px: P={p:.3f} R={r:.3f}")

    # --- 2. synthetic scene with exact ground-truth edges, three noise levels
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:256, 0:256]
    scene = np.full((256, 256), 80.0)
    scene[(yy - 100) ** 2 + (xx - 90) ** 2 < 60 ** 2] = 170
    scene[150:230, 140:240] = 120
    scene[40:90, 170:230] = 30
    lab = np.zeros(scene.shape, int)
    lab[scene == 170], lab[scene == 120], lab[scene == 30] = 1, 2, 3
    gt = np.zeros_like(lab, bool)                     # GT edge = label changes to the right/below
    gt[:, :-1] |= lab[:, :-1] != lab[:, 1:]
    gt[:-1, :] |= lab[:-1, :] != lab[1:, :]
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    print(f"{'noise sd':>8} | {'Sobel |g|>120':>16} | {'LoG s=3 zero-x':>16} | {'Canny s=1.5':>16} | {'Canny s=3':>16}")
    for sd in (5, 20, 40):
        img = scene + rng.normal(0, sd, scene.shape)
        gx, gy = sobel(img)
        rows = [score(np.hypot(gx, gy) > 120, gt),        # fixed parameters at every noise level
                score(log_edges(img, 3.0, 0.5), gt),
                score(canny(img, 1.5, 15, 40), gt),
                score(canny(img, 3.0, 15, 40), gt)]
        print(f"{sd:>8} | " + " | ".join(f"P{a:.2f} R{b:.2f} F{c:.2f}" for a, b, c in rows))
camera: ours 7305 edge px, cv2.Canny 7315 px; agreement within 1 px: P=0.998 R=0.998 noise sd | Sobel |g|>120 | LoG s=3 zero-x | Canny s=1.5 | Canny s=3 5 | P0.98 R1.00 F0.99 | P1.00 R0.98 F0.99 | P1.00 R1.00 F1.00 | P0.99 R0.98 F0.98 20 | P0.12 R0.99 F0.22 | P0.98 R0.92 F0.95 | P0.19 R0.99 F0.32 | P0.99 R0.97 F0.98 40 | P0.05 R1.00 F0.10 | P0.31 R0.86 F0.45 | P0.05 R0.97 F0.10 | P0.96 R0.98 F0.97

The first line checks the implementation: on the cameraman image, 99.8% of our Canny edge pixels lie within one pixel of an OpenCV edge pixel and vice versa (the remaining differences come from how the two implementations bin gradient directions). The table scores each detector against the true boundaries of a synthetic scene, with all parameters fixed across noise levels. With little noise every detector is near perfect. At noise standard deviation 20, a plain gradient threshold fires on 88% wrong pixels (precision 0.12) and so does Canny with a small σ, while Canny with σ = 3 still scores F = 0.98. The parameter that matters is the scale of the smoothing, not the cleverness of the later steps. LoG zero crossings degrade sooner, at noise 40, because the second derivative is more sensitive to noise than the first. Figure 4 shows the same contrast visually.

Choosing Canny's thresholdsThe high threshold should sit above the gradient magnitude produced by noise alone and the low threshold at a third to a half of it, the 2:1 to 3:1 ratio Canny recommended [11]. Both are in units of gradient magnitude, which depends on image contrast and on the derivative filter, so thresholds copied from another pipeline often fail. A robust habit is to set them from the statistics of the image, for example from a percentile of the smoothed gradient magnitude, and to choose σ from the noise level before touching the thresholds.
Exercises · §2
  1. An ideal vertical step edge of contrast c grey levels is filtered with Sx. What is the peak response? What contrast does the threshold |∇I| > 120 in edges.py correspond to?
    Show solution

    At the pixel just before the step, the right column of the kernel sees intensity c higher than the left column, so the response is (1 + 2 + 1)c = 4c. The threshold 120 therefore corresponds to a step of 30 grey levels, which is why it finds all three boundaries (contrasts 40, 50 and 90) in the clean image.

  2. Explain the collapse of the Sobel threshold at noise standard deviation 20 quantitatively. Treat Ix and Iy on a flat region as independent zero-mean Gaussians, and compute the fraction of background pixels whose |∇I| exceeds 120.
    Show solution

    The squared weights of Sx sum to 1 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 4 + 1 = 12, so with pixel noise σn = 20 each derivative has standard deviation √12 × 20 ≈ 69.3. The magnitude of two independent Gaussians with that spread follows a Rayleigh distribution, so P(|∇I| > t) = exp(−t²/2 × 69.3²) = exp(−1.50) ≈ 0.22. More than a fifth of the 60,000-odd background pixels pass the threshold, against fewer than 1,000 true edge pixels, which matches the measured precision of 0.12.

  3. Non-maximum suppression in edges.py quantises the gradient direction into four bins. What is the largest angular error this introduces, and how do production implementations reduce it?
    Show solution

    The bins are 45° wide and centred on 0°, 45°, 90° and 135°, so a direction can be off by up to 22.5°. Implementations either interpolate the gradient magnitude at the two exact points one pixel along the gradient direction (bilinear interpolation between neighbours) or, like OpenCV, use a fast integer test of which octant the gradient lies in, which has the same quantisation but avoids floating-point maths [1].

  4. Show that the difference of Gaussians G(kσ) − G(σ) is approximately (k − 1)σ² ∇²G. Why is the factor σ² useful rather than a nuisance?
    Show solution

    The Gaussian satisfies the heat equation ∂G/∂σ = σ∇²G. A finite difference in σ gives ∂G/∂σ ≈ [G(kσ) − G(σ)]/(kσ − σ), so G(kσ) − G(σ) ≈ (k − 1)σ²∇²G. The factor σ² is exactly the scale normalisation needed to compare Laplacian responses across scales [7], so a DoG pyramid with a constant ratio k between levels is automatically scale-normalised, which is what SIFT exploits [13].

§3Feature detection: corners, blobs and interest points

To match two images we need points that can be found again: positions that are well localised in both directions and that a detector will pick out again after the viewpoint, lighting or scale changes. Points along an edge fail the first test, because they can slide along the edge without changing the local appearance (the aperture problem again, see §7). Corners and blobs pass it.

3.1 Corners: the structure tensor

Moravec measured how much a small window changes when shifted in a few directions [14]. Harris and Stephens made this continuous: for a shift (u, v), a first-order Taylor expansion gives the weighted sum of squared differences

E(u, v) ≈ [u v] M [u v]ᵀ, M = Σ_w w(x, y) ⎡ I_x² I_x I_y ⎤ ⎣ I_x I_y I_y² ⎦

where w is a Gaussian window. The structure tensor M summarises the gradients in the window. Its two eigenvalues λ₁ ≥ λ₂ measure the change for shifts along its eigenvectors: both small means a flat region, one large and one small means an edge, and both large means a corner (Figure 5). Harris avoided the eigen-decomposition with the response R = det M − k (tr M)² = λ₁λ₂ − k(λ₁ + λ₂)², with k ≈ 0.04 to 0.06 [15]. Shi and Tomasi showed that the smaller eigenvalue λ₂ is the right criterion when the points are to be tracked, because it bounds how well the tracking equations of §7 are conditioned [16]; it is OpenCV's goodFeaturesToTrack.

3.2 Fast corners

FAST (features from accelerated segment test) skips derivatives entirely. A pixel is a corner if at least n contiguous pixels on a 16-pixel circle of radius 3 around it are all brighter, or all darker, than the centre by a threshold; n = 9 works best. Rosten and Drummond learned a decision tree that orders the pixel tests so that most non-corners are rejected after two or three comparisons, which made FAST several times faster than Harris or the DoG detector [17]. FAST has no notion of scale or orientation, which ORB adds (§4).

3.3 Blobs and automatic scale selection

A corner detector works at one scale. To find the same structure in a zoomed image, the detector must also choose a scale for each point. Lindeberg showed that this can be done by looking for extrema over scale of scale-normalised derivatives: for a blob, the response σ²|∇²L| peaks at a σ proportional to the blob's size, and that σ becomes the point's characteristic scale [7]. For a disc of radius r the peak is at σ = r/√2, which the code below confirms.

Lowe's SIFT detector applies this idea efficiently: build a Gaussian pyramid with several scales per octave, subtract adjacent levels to obtain a difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) stack, find points that are larger or smaller than all 26 neighbours in space and scale, refine their position to sub-pixel and sub-scale accuracy by fitting a quadratic, and discard low-contrast points and points on edges, where the ratio of principal curvatures (from the 2 × 2 Hessian) exceeds 10 [13]. Each keypoint then gets a dominant orientation from a histogram of gradient directions around it, so that the descriptor (§4) can be computed in a rotated frame. Mikolajczyk and Schmid extended scale selection to affine-covariant regions (Harris-Affine, Hessian-Affine) that survive large viewpoint changes [18]. Maximally stable extremal regions (MSER) take a different route: they are connected components of thresholded images whose area stays almost constant over a wide range of thresholds, and they are covariant to affine changes of geometry and monotonic changes of intensity [19]. Systematic comparisons of these detectors are given by Mikolajczyk et al. and by Tuytelaars and Mikolajczyk [20,21].

detectors.pyHarris from scratch, scale selection, repeatability under rotation and zoom ran

"""Interest points: Harris from scratch, automatic scale selection, and a repeatability test."""
import numpy as np
import cv2
from scipy import ndimage as ndi
from skimage import data


def harris_response(img, sigma_d=1.0, sigma_i=2.0, k=0.04):
    """R = det(M) - k trace(M)^2, M = Gaussian-weighted structure tensor."""
    sm = ndi.gaussian_filter(img, sigma_d)
    Iy, Ix = np.gradient(sm)
    Sxx = ndi.gaussian_filter(Ix * Ix, sigma_i)
    Syy = ndi.gaussian_filter(Iy * Iy, sigma_i)
    Sxy = ndi.gaussian_filter(Ix * Iy, sigma_i)
    det, tr = Sxx * Syy - Sxy ** 2, Sxx + Syy
    lam_min = tr / 2 - np.sqrt((tr / 2) ** 2 - det)        # Shi-Tomasi score, for comparison
    return det - k * tr ** 2, lam_min


def local_maxima(R, n, radius=4):
    """Top-n local maxima of R (non-maximum suppression in a (2r+1)^2 window)."""
    peaks = (R == ndi.maximum_filter(R, size=2 * radius + 1)) & (R > 0)
    ys, xs = np.nonzero(peaks)
    order = np.argsort(R[ys, xs])[::-1][:n]
    return np.stack([xs[order], ys[order]], 1).astype(np.float32)


def characteristic_scale(img, x, y, sigmas):
    """Scale-normalised LoG response sigma^2 |LoG| at one point, over a range of sigma."""
    return np.array([s ** 2 * abs(ndi.gaussian_laplace(img, s)[y, x]) for s in sigmas])


def repeatability(pts_a, pts_b, H, shape_b, tol=2.5):
    """Fraction of A's points (that land inside B) with a B detection within tol pixels."""
    pa = cv2.perspectiveTransform(pts_a.reshape(-1, 1, 2), H).reshape(-1, 2)
    inside = (pa[:, 0] >= 8) & (pa[:, 1] >= 8) & (pa[:, 0] < shape_b[1] - 8) & (pa[:, 1] < shape_b[0] - 8)
    pa = pa[inside]
    d = np.linalg.norm(pa[:, None, :] - pts_b[None, :, :], axis=2)
    return (d.min(1) <= tol).mean(), len(pa)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # 1. Harris from scratch agrees with OpenCV on where the corners are
    img = data.camera().astype(np.float32) / 255
    R, lam = harris_response(img)
    ours = local_maxima(R, 300)
    cvR = cv2.cornerHarris(cv2.GaussianBlur(img, (0, 0), 1.0), blockSize=5, ksize=3, k=0.04)
    theirs = local_maxima(cvR, 300)
    d = np.linalg.norm(ours[:, None] - theirs[None], axis=2).min(1)
    print(f"Harris top-300: {np.mean(d <= 2):.0%} of ours lie within 2 px of an OpenCV corner")

    # 2. automatic scale selection: blobs of radius r peak at sigma = r / sqrt(2)
    sigmas = np.linspace(1, 20, 96)
    for r in (4, 8, 16):
        yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:128, 0:128]
        blob = ((yy - 64) ** 2 + (xx - 64) ** 2 <= r ** 2).astype(float)
        s_hat = sigmas[np.argmax(characteristic_scale(blob, 64, 64, sigmas))]
        print(f"disc radius {r:2d}: peak at sigma = {s_hat:5.2f}  (r/sqrt2 = {r/np.sqrt(2):5.2f})")

    # 3. repeatability under rotation by 30 degrees and scaling by 0.7
    g8 = data.camera()
    h, w = g8.shape
    A = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D((w / 2, h / 2), 30, 0.7)
    H = np.vstack([A, [0, 0, 1]])
    g8b = cv2.warpAffine(g8, A, (w, h), flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)
    N = 500

    def harris_pts(g):
        return local_maxima(harris_response(g.astype(np.float32) / 255)[0], N)

    def shi_pts(g):
        return local_maxima(harris_response(g.astype(np.float32) / 255)[1], N)

    def cv_pts(det):
        def f(g):
            kps = sorted(det.detect(g, None), key=lambda k: -k.response)[:N]
            return np.float32([k.pt for k in kps])
        return f

    dets = {"Harris": harris_pts, "Shi-Tomasi": shi_pts,
            "FAST-9": cv_pts(cv2.FastFeatureDetector_create(threshold=20)),
            "SIFT (DoG)": cv_pts(cv2.SIFT_create(nfeatures=N)),
            "ORB (FAST+pyr)": cv_pts(cv2.ORB_create(nfeatures=N))}
    print(f"{'detector':<15} {'rot 30, x1.0':>13} {'rot 30, x0.7':>13}")
    A1 = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D((w / 2, h / 2), 30, 1.0)
    H1 = np.vstack([A1, [0, 0, 1]])
    g8c = cv2.warpAffine(g8, A1, (w, h), flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)
    for name, f in dets.items():
        pa = f(g8)
        r1, _ = repeatability(pa, f(g8c), H1, g8c.shape)
        r2, _ = repeatability(pa, f(g8b), H, g8b.shape)
        print(f"{name:<15} {r1:>13.2f} {r2:>13.2f}")
Harris top-300: 82% of ours lie within 2 px of an OpenCV corner disc radius 4: peak at sigma = 2.80 (r/sqrt2 = 2.83) disc radius 8: peak at sigma = 5.60 (r/sqrt2 = 5.66) disc radius 16: peak at sigma = 11.20 (r/sqrt2 = 11.31) detector rot 30, x1.0 rot 30, x0.7 Harris 0.86 0.41 Shi-Tomasi 0.85 0.42 FAST-9 0.77 0.66 SIFT (DoG) 0.69 0.56 ORB (FAST+pyr) 0.90 0.92

Our Harris implementation and OpenCV's pick essentially the same corners (82% within 2 pixels; the rest differ because OpenCV sums the tensor in a box window with Sobel derivatives while we use a Gaussian window with central differences). Scale selection lands on r/√2 for all three discs to within the 0.2 grid step of σ. The repeatability test measures the fraction of points detected in the original image that are detected again, within 2.5 pixels, after rotating the image by 30° and optionally shrinking it to 0.7 of its size. All detectors cope reasonably with pure rotation, because the structure tensor and FAST's circle are both rotation-invariant. Under the zoom, the single-scale Harris and Shi–Tomasi detectors lose more than half their points, while the multi-scale ORB keeps 92%. SIFT scores lower than its reputation here because this simple protocol measures position only, at a fixed 2.5-pixel tolerance: SIFT points detected at coarse scales are located less precisely in pixels, although their regions overlap well. The standard protocol scores the overlap of the detected regions instead [20]; Exercise 3 asks why that is fairer.

Exercises · §3
  1. Compute the Harris response with k = 0.04 for structure tensors diag(10, 0.1) and diag(5, 4). Classify each window.
    Show solution

    For diag(10, 0.1): det = 1, trace = 10.1, so R = 1 − 0.04 × 102.01 = −3.08 < 0, an edge (gradient mostly in one direction). For diag(5, 4): det = 20, trace = 9, so R = 20 − 0.04 × 81 = 16.76 > 0, a corner. The Shi–Tomasi scores are 0.1 and 4, giving the same ranking.

  2. The FAST paper's high-speed pre-test examines only the four compass pixels 1, 5, 9 and 13 of the 16-pixel circle and rejects the candidate unless at least three of them pass. Why is this test exact for n = 12 but not for n = 9?
    Show solution

    The four compass pixels are spaced four apart on the circle. Any arc of L contiguous pixels contains at least ⌊L/4⌋ of them. An arc of 12 contains at least three, so a corner by the 12-pixel criterion always passes the pre-test, and the test never rejects a true corner. An arc of 9 is only guaranteed to contain two, so the three-of-four test could reject a valid FAST-9 corner. This is one reason Rosten and Drummond replaced the hand-made test with a learned decision tree [17].

  3. In the repeatability table SIFT keeps 56% of its points under zoom by position alone. Why does scoring the overlap of the detected regions (scale circles or ellipses) give a fairer comparison for scale-invariant detectors?
    Show solution

    A keypoint at scale σ describes a region about 6σ across, and its position is only meaningful to a fraction of σ. A point detected at σ = 8 that is off by 3 pixels still describes almost the same region, and its descriptor will still match; a fixed pixel tolerance counts it as a failure while a single-scale detector's fine points pass easily. The region-overlap criterion (for example, intersection over union of the two regions above 60% after mapping one into the other image) compares what the descriptor actually sees [20].

  4. A detector finds a bright blob whose scale-normalised LoG response peaks at σ = 6. Estimate the blob's radius. In a SIFT pyramid with base σ₀ = 1.6 and octaves doubling σ, in which octave is it found?
    Show solution

    The radius is about √2 × 6 ≈ 8.5 pixels. Octave o covers σ from 1.6 × 2o to 1.6 × 2o+1; σ/1.6 = 3.75 lies between 2 and 4, so the blob is found in octave 1 (counting the original resolution as octave 0), where the image is downsampled by 2. Lowe's implementation first doubles the input image, which adds an octave −1 for small structures [13].

§4Feature descriptors: SIFT, SURF, BRIEF, ORB and HOG

A detector says where a distinctive point is; a descriptor says what it looks like, as a vector that should be nearly the same for the same physical point seen in another image and different for other points. The design problem is to be invariant to the changes we expect (brightness and contrast, small shifts, rotation and scale once the detector has normalised them) while staying discriminative. Two families dominate: histograms of gradient orientations, compared with Euclidean distance, and binary strings of intensity comparisons, compared with Hamming distance.

4.1 SIFT

SIFT samples gradients in a 16 × 16 grid around the keypoint, rotated to the keypoint's orientation and scaled to its scale, weights them by a Gaussian centred on the point, and accumulates them into a 4 × 4 array of orientation histograms with 8 bins each, using trilinear interpolation so that small shifts move votes smoothly between bins. The resulting 128 numbers are normalised to unit length, values above 0.2 are clipped to reduce the influence of large gradients from non-linear lighting effects, and the vector is renormalised [13]. Figure 7 shows the layout. In the evaluation of Mikolajczyk and Schmid, SIFT and its variant GLOH were the most distinctive descriptors across viewpoint, blur, compression and illumination changes [22]. A simple improvement, RootSIFT, L1-normalises the vector and takes element-wise square roots, so that Euclidean distance between RootSIFT vectors corresponds to the Hellinger kernel between the original histograms; it improved retrieval at no cost [23]. SIFT was patented in the United States until 2020, after which OpenCV moved it from the contributed modules into the main library [24].

4.2 SURF

SURF (speeded-up robust features) made the same pipeline faster with integral images. Its detector uses the determinant of the Hessian, with the second-derivative Gaussians replaced by box filters (the 9 × 9 filter approximates σ = 1.2), so filters at every scale cost the same four lookups per box and the image never has to be downsampled. Its descriptor sums Haar-wavelet responses dx, dy, |dx| and |dy| over a 4 × 4 grid, giving 64 values [25]. SURF is still patented and is not built into the standard OpenCV wheels; calling cv2.xfeatures2d.SURF_create in the version used here raises a "patented, not implemented" error, so the code below reproduces its key ingredient, the box-filter derivative, instead.

4.3 BRIEF and ORB

BRIEF smooths the patch and performs 256 intensity comparisons between pixel pairs drawn once from an isotropic Gaussian around the centre; each comparison gives one bit [26]. A descriptor is 32 bytes and two are compared with an XOR and a population count, which is far cheaper than a 128-dimensional Euclidean distance. BRIEF has no rotation invariance: rotate the patch and the pairs sample different pixels. ORB (oriented FAST and rotated BRIEF) fixes this by assigning each FAST keypoint an orientation from its intensity centroid, rotating the sampling pattern accordingly ("steered BRIEF"), and choosing the 256 pairs by a greedy search for tests that are uncorrelated and have high variance; it also detects on a pyramid for scale invariance [27]. BRISK and AKAZE are other binary descriptors in OpenCV, with sampling patterns and nonlinear scale spaces of their own [28,29].

4.4 HOG

Histograms of oriented gradients describe a whole window rather than a keypoint. Dalal and Triggs divided a 64 × 128 pedestrian window into 8 × 8 cells, built a 9-bin histogram of unsigned gradient orientations in each, normalised every 2 × 2 block of cells (overlapping, with stride one cell) with L2-Hys (normalise, clip at 0.2, renormalise), and concatenated the blocks: 7 × 15 blocks × 36 values = 3,780 features, fed to a linear SVM [30]. Fine orientation binning, coarse spatial binning and strong local contrast normalisation were the ingredients they found essential. HOG with a sliding window was the reference pedestrian detector for most of the following decade.

descriptors.pyHOG and BRIEF from scratch, SURF's box filter, rotation invariance ran

"""Descriptors: HOG and BRIEF from scratch, SURF's box-filter Hessian, and invariance to rotation."""
import numpy as np
import cv2
from scipy import ndimage as ndi
from skimage import data
from skimage.feature import hog as sk_hog


def hog(img, cell=8, block=2, nbins=9, eps=1e-5):
    """Dalal-Triggs HOG: unsigned gradients, 9 bins over 0-180 deg, L2-Hys block normalisation."""
    img = img.astype(np.float64)
    gx = np.zeros_like(img); gy = np.zeros_like(img)
    gx[:, 1:-1] = img[:, 2:] - img[:, :-2]                  # centred [-1, 0, 1] differences
    gy[1:-1, :] = img[2:, :] - img[:-2, :]
    mag = np.hypot(gx, gy)
    ang = np.rad2deg(np.arctan2(gy, gx)) % 180
    ch, cw = img.shape[0] // cell, img.shape[1] // cell
    hist = np.zeros((ch, cw, nbins))
    b = np.minimum((ang / (180 / nbins)).astype(int), nbins - 1)
    for i in range(nbins):                                   # magnitude-weighted votes per cell
        m = np.where(b == i, mag, 0)[:ch * cell, :cw * cell]
        hist[..., i] = m.reshape(ch, cell, cw, cell).sum((1, 3))
    feats = []
    for y in range(ch - block + 1):
        for x in range(cw - block + 1):
            v = hist[y:y + block, x:x + block].ravel()
            v = v / np.sqrt((v ** 2).sum() + eps ** 2)
            v = np.minimum(v, 0.2)                           # "Hys": clip, then renormalise
            feats.append(v / np.sqrt((v ** 2).sum() + eps ** 2))
    return np.concatenate(feats)


class Brief:
    """BRIEF: 256 intensity comparisons between Gaussian-sampled pixel pairs of a smoothed patch."""

    def __init__(self, patch=31, nbits=256, seed=0):
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        half = patch // 2
        p = np.clip(np.round(rng.normal(0, patch / 5, (nbits, 4))), -half, half).astype(int)
        self.pairs, self.half = p, half

    def compute(self, img, pts):
        sm = cv2.GaussianBlur(img, (9, 9), 2)
        keep = [(x, y) for x, y in np.round(pts).astype(int)
                if self.half <= x < img.shape[1] - self.half and self.half <= y < img.shape[0] - self.half]
        p = self.pairs
        bits = np.array([sm[y + p[:, 1], x + p[:, 0]] < sm[y + p[:, 3], x + p[:, 2]] for x, y in keep])
        return np.array(keep, np.float32), np.packbits(bits, axis=1)   # 256 bits = 32 bytes


def surf_box_dxx(img, s=9):
    """SURF's 9x9 box approximation of d2/dx2 at sigma 1.2: lobes +1, -2, +1, built from box sums."""
    ii = np.pad(img.cumsum(0).cumsum(1), ((1, 0), (1, 0)))
    def box(y0, x0, y1, x1):          # sums over [y0,y1) x [x0,x1) centred at every pixel, via shifts
        H, W = img.shape
        P = np.pad(ii, s, mode="edge")                       # = zero image outside the border
        f = lambda dy, dx: P[s + dy:s + dy + H, s + dx:s + dx + W]
        return f(y1, x1) - f(y0, x1) - f(y1, x0) + f(y0, x0)
    l = s // 3                                               # lobe width 3, height 5 for s = 9
    hy, hx, hm = (2 * l - 1) // 2, (3 * l) // 2, l // 2      # half-height 2, half-widths 4 and 1
    whole = box(-hy, -hx, hy + 1, hx + 1)
    mid = box(-hy, -hm, hy + 1, hm + 1)
    return (whole - 3 * mid) / s ** 2                        # +1 outer lobes, -2 middle lobe


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # 1. HOG from scratch vs scikit-image on a 128 x 64 window (the pedestrian-detector size)
    win = data.astronaut()[60:188, 180:244].mean(2)
    ours = hog(win)
    ref = sk_hog(win, orientations=9, pixels_per_cell=(8, 8), cells_per_block=(2, 2),
                 block_norm="L2-Hys", feature_vector=True)
    print(f"HOG length ours {ours.size}, skimage {ref.size}; max |diff| {np.abs(ours - ref).max():.1e}")

    # 2. SURF's box filter tracks the Gaussian second derivative it replaces
    cam = data.camera().astype(np.float64) / 255
    box = surf_box_dxx(cam)
    gauss = ndi.gaussian_filter(cam, 1.2, order=(0, 2))
    print(f"SURF 9x9 box Dxx vs Gaussian d2/dx2 (sigma 1.2): correlation {np.corrcoef(box.ravel(), gauss.ravel())[0, 1]:.3f}")

    # 3. rotation: nearest-neighbour matching accuracy against ground truth
    g = data.camera()
    h, w = g.shape
    orb = cv2.ORB_create(nfeatures=800)
    sift = cv2.SIFT_create(nfeatures=800)
    brief = Brief()

    def nn_accuracy(pa, da, pb, db, H, norm):
        """Among A's points that were re-detected in B, how often is the nearest descriptor the right one?"""
        proj = cv2.perspectiveTransform(pa.reshape(-1, 1, 2), H).reshape(-1, 2)
        d = np.linalg.norm(proj[:, None] - pb[None], axis=2)
        matchable = d.min(1) < 3
        ms = cv2.BFMatcher(norm).match(da[matchable], db)
        err = d[matchable][np.arange(len(ms)), [m.trainIdx for m in ms]]
        return np.mean(err < 3)

    print(f"{'angle':>5} | {'BRIEF (ours)':>12} | {'ORB':>6} | {'SIFT':>6}")
    for ang in (0, 10, 20, 45, 90):
        A = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D((w / 2, h / 2), ang, 1.0)
        H = np.vstack([A, [0, 0, 1]])
        gb = cv2.warpAffine(g, A, (w, h))
        row = []
        # BRIEF on the same FAST keypoints that ORB uses, but without orientation
        ka = np.float32([k.pt for k in orb.detect(g, None)])
        kb = np.float32([k.pt for k in orb.detect(gb, None)])
        pa, da = brief.compute(g, ka); pb, db = brief.compute(gb, kb)
        row.append(nn_accuracy(pa, da, pb, db, H, cv2.NORM_HAMMING))
        for det, norm in ((orb, cv2.NORM_HAMMING), (sift, cv2.NORM_L2)):
            ka, da = det.detectAndCompute(g, None); kb, db = det.detectAndCompute(gb, None)
            row.append(nn_accuracy(np.float32([k.pt for k in ka]), da, np.float32([k.pt for k in kb]), db, H, norm))
        print(f"{ang:>5} | {row[0]:>12.2f} | {row[1]:>6.2f} | {row[2]:>6.2f}")
    print("descriptor sizes: SIFT 128 float32 = 512 B, ORB/BRIEF 256 bits = 32 B, HOG window", ours.size, "floats")
HOG length ours 3780, skimage 3780; max |diff| 5.0e-08 SURF 9x9 box Dxx vs Gaussian d2/dx2 (sigma 1.2): correlation 0.846 angle | BRIEF (ours) | ORB | SIFT 0 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 10 | 0.94 | 0.86 | 0.88 20 | 0.64 | 0.88 | 0.86 45 | 0.01 | 0.84 | 0.84 90 | 0.00 | 0.86 | 0.98 descriptor sizes: SIFT 128 float32 = 512 B, ORB/BRIEF 256 bits = 32 B, HOG window 3780 floats

The HOG implementation matches scikit-image's to floating-point precision, and SURF's crude 9 × 9 box filter correlates at 0.85 with the true Gaussian second derivative, which is enough for detection. The rotation table measures how often the nearest descriptor in the rotated image is the correct point, among points that the detector found in both images. Plain BRIEF works for small rotations and fails completely by 45°. ORB and SIFT hold up at all angles; SIFT scores 0.98 at 90° because a 90° rotation maps pixels exactly onto pixels and introduces no interpolation, while ORB's orientation estimate from the intensity centroid is coarser.

Exercises · §4
  1. Verify the HOG length of 3,780 for a 64 × 128 window with 8 × 8 cells, 2 × 2 blocks and 9 bins. How long is the descriptor for a 96 × 160 window?
    Show solution

    There are 8 × 16 cells and, with a stride of one cell, 7 × 15 = 105 blocks of 2 × 2 × 9 = 36 values: 3,780. A 96 × 160 window has 12 × 20 cells, 11 × 19 = 209 blocks and 7,524 values.

  2. Two unrelated 256-bit BRIEF descriptors behave roughly like independent fair coin flips. What are the mean and standard deviation of their Hamming distance? A matching threshold of 64 is how many standard deviations below the mean?
    Show solution

    The distance is approximately Binomial(256, 0.5): mean 128, standard deviation √(256 × 0.25) = 8. A distance of 64 is 8 standard deviations below the mean, so chance matches below it are vanishingly rare; in practice bits are correlated and the distribution is wider, which is why ORB selected uncorrelated tests [27].

  3. SURF's 9 × 9 box filter approximates a Gaussian second derivative with σ = 1.2. Which σ does the 15 × 15 filter approximate, and how does its cost compare with the 9 × 9 filter's?
    Show solution

    The scale grows in proportion to the filter size: σ = 1.2 × 15/9 = 2.0. Each lobe is still one box, so with an integral image the cost is the same handful of lookups per pixel at every scale [25]. A Gaussian derivative filter at σ = 2 would need about four times as many taps per dimension as at σ = 1.2 for the same truncation.

  4. Show that Euclidean distance between RootSIFT vectors is a monotonic function of the Hellinger kernel between the L1-normalised SIFT histograms x and y.
    Show solution

    RootSIFT is x' = √x element-wise, with Σx = 1, so ‖x'‖² = Σx = 1. Then ‖x' − y'‖² = 1 + 1 − 2 Σ√(xiyi) = 2 − 2H(x, y), where H is the Hellinger (Bhattacharyya) kernel. Nearest neighbours under L2 on RootSIFT are therefore nearest neighbours under the Hellinger kernel, which suits histograms better than L2 because it damps the influence of large bins [23].

§5Feature matching: nearest neighbours and the ratio test

Given descriptors a1…aN from image A and b1…bM from image B, the obvious match for ai is its nearest neighbour in B. Most nearest neighbours are wrong, however, because many points in A have no counterpart in B (they are occluded, outside the view, or not re-detected). Three filters are in common use.

  • A distance threshold keeps matches with ‖a − b‖ below a fixed value. It works poorly because descriptor distances vary a lot between image regions: a correct match in a low-contrast area can be farther than a wrong one in a textured area.
  • Cross-checking (mutual nearest neighbours) keeps i → j only if i is also the nearest neighbour of j in A.
  • Lowe's ratio test compares the nearest distance d1 with the second-nearest d2 and keeps the match only if d1/d2 < τ, typically 0.7 to 0.8. A correct match should be much closer than the best wrong one, while for a point with no true counterpart the nearest and second-nearest are both random and similar. Lowe reported that τ = 0.8 removed 90% of false matches while discarding fewer than 5% of correct ones [13].

For large databases, exact search is replaced by approximate nearest-neighbour search: randomised k-d trees and priority search k-means trees for real-valued descriptors, and locality-sensitive hashing or hierarchical clustering for binary ones, all available in the FLANN library that OpenCV wraps [31].

matching.pyratio test from scratch, filtering rules scored against the true homography, exact vs approximate search ran

"""Descriptor matching: nearest neighbours, cross-checking, Lowe's ratio test, and approximate search."""
import time
import numpy as np
import cv2
from skimage import data


def make_pair(seed=0):
    """Image A and a perspective-warped, re-lit, noisy copy B with the true homography H (A -> B)."""
    a = cv2.cvtColor(data.astronaut(), cv2.COLOR_RGB2GRAY)
    h, w = a.shape
    src = np.float32([[0, 0], [w, 0], [w, h], [0, h]])
    dst = np.float32([[40, 60], [w - 20, 15], [w - 70, h - 30], [25, h - 70]])
    H = cv2.getPerspectiveTransform(src, dst)
    b = cv2.warpPerspective(a, H, (w, h)).astype(np.float32)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    b = np.clip(0.8 * b + 25 + rng.normal(0, 6, b.shape), 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
    return a, b, H


def match_ratio(da, db, ratio=0.8, cross_check=False):
    """From-scratch matcher on squared L2: keep i -> j if d1 < ratio * d2 (and optionally j -> i)."""
    D = (da ** 2).sum(1)[:, None] + (db ** 2).sum(1)[None, :] - 2 * da @ db.T
    D = np.sqrt(np.maximum(D, 0))
    nn = np.argsort(D, axis=1)[:, :2]
    d1, d2 = D[np.arange(len(da)), nn[:, 0]], D[np.arange(len(da)), nn[:, 1]]
    keep = d1 < ratio * d2
    if cross_check:
        keep &= D.argmin(0)[nn[:, 0]] == np.arange(len(da))
    return np.nonzero(keep)[0], nn[keep, 0]


def correct(pa, pb, H, tol=3.0):
    proj = cv2.perspectiveTransform(pa.reshape(-1, 1, 2), H).reshape(-1, 2)
    return np.linalg.norm(proj - pb, axis=1) < tol


if __name__ == "__main__":
    a, b, H = make_pair()
    sift = cv2.SIFT_create(nfeatures=2000)
    ka, da = sift.detectAndCompute(a, None); kb, db = sift.detectAndCompute(b, None)
    pa = np.float32([k.pt for k in ka]); pb = np.float32([k.pt for k in kb])
    print(f"SIFT keypoints: A {len(ka)}, B {len(kb)}")

    # 1. our matcher agrees with OpenCV's knnMatch + ratio test
    i, j = match_ratio(da, db, 0.8)
    knn = cv2.BFMatcher(cv2.NORM_L2).knnMatch(da, db, k=2)
    cv_pairs = {(m.queryIdx, m.trainIdx) for m, n in knn if m.distance < 0.8 * n.distance}
    print(f"ratio 0.8: ours {len(i)} matches, OpenCV {len(cv_pairs)}, identical {len(cv_pairs & set(zip(i, j)))}")

    # 2. precision and number of correct matches for each filtering rule
    print(f"{'rule':<26} {'kept':>5} {'correct':>8} {'precision':>10}")
    rules = [("nearest neighbour only", 1.01, False), ("cross-check", 1.01, True),
             ("ratio < 0.9", 0.9, False), ("ratio < 0.8", 0.8, False),
             ("ratio < 0.7", 0.7, False), ("ratio < 0.8 + cross-check", 0.8, True)]
    for name, r, cc in rules:
        i, j = match_ratio(da, db, r, cc)
        ok = correct(pa[i], pb[j], H)
        print(f"{name:<26} {len(i):>5} {ok.sum():>8} {ok.mean():>10.3f}")

    # 3. why a ratio beats an absolute distance threshold
    i, j = match_ratio(da, db, 1.01)
    D = np.linalg.norm(da[i] - db[j], axis=1)
    ok = correct(pa[i], pb[j], H)
    for t in (150, 200, 250):
        kept = D < t
        print(f"absolute distance < {t}: kept {kept.sum():4d}, precision {ok[kept].mean():.3f}")

    # 4. exact vs approximate nearest neighbours on a larger database (SIFT from several images)
    gray = lambda im: cv2.cvtColor(im, cv2.COLOR_RGB2GRAY) if im.ndim == 3 else im
    db_all = np.vstack([cv2.SIFT_create().detectAndCompute(gray(f()), None)[1]
                        for f in (data.coffee, data.rocket, data.camera, data.brick, data.gravel, data.grass,
                                  data.hubble_deep_field, data.chelsea, data.coins, data.moon)] + [db])
    good_q, _ = match_ratio(da, db, 0.8)                     # queries with a distinctive match
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); bf = cv2.BFMatcher(cv2.NORM_L2).knnMatch(da, db_all, k=1); t_bf = time.perf_counter() - t0
    for checks in (16, 64, 256):
        flann = cv2.FlannBasedMatcher({"algorithm": 1, "trees": 4}, {"checks": checks})   # randomised kd-trees
        flann.add([db_all]); flann.train()
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); fl = flann.knnMatch(da, k=1); t_fl = time.perf_counter() - t0
        same = np.array([m[0].trainIdx == f[0].trainIdx for m, f in zip(bf, fl)])
        print(f"{len(da)} queries x {len(db_all)}: brute force {t_bf*1e3:.0f} ms,"
              f" FLANN checks={checks:<3} {t_fl*1e3:3.0f} ms, same NN {same.mean():.1%}"
              f" (ratio-test survivors: {same[good_q].mean():.1%})")

    orb = cv2.ORB_create(nfeatures=2000)
    ka, da = orb.detectAndCompute(a, None); kb, db = orb.detectAndCompute(b, None)
    pa = np.float32([k.pt for k in ka]); pb = np.float32([k.pt for k in kb])
    knn = cv2.BFMatcher(cv2.NORM_HAMMING).knnMatch(da, db, k=2)
    good = [m for m, n in knn if m.distance < 0.8 * n.distance]
    ok = correct(pa[[m.queryIdx for m in good]], pb[[m.trainIdx for m in good]], H)
    print(f"ORB (Hamming) ratio 0.8: kept {len(good)}, correct {ok.sum()}, precision {ok.mean():.3f}")

Image B is the astronaut image under a known perspective warp, a contrast change and noise, so every match can be checked against the true homography. Plain nearest neighbours are right only 43% of the time. Cross-checking lifts precision to 0.82, the ratio test at 0.8 to 0.93, and the two combined to 0.97 while keeping 438 of the 477 correct matches. A distance threshold does worse than the ratio at every operating point: at 385 kept matches its precision (0.925) is below that of the ratio test keeping 440 (0.968). Figure 9 shows why: the distances of correct and wrong matches overlap heavily, while their ratios barely do. The approximate search results make a subtler point. FLANN with 64 checks returns the exact nearest neighbour for only 77% of all queries, but for 98% of the queries that pass the ratio test, which are the only ones that matter. Distinctive matches are easy to find approximately [31].
